title: Uniform Circular Motion and Gravitation
learning_objectives: Define the angle turned, the angular velocity and the angular acceleration.
Explain centripetal acceleration and centripetal force, and give them a direction.
State Newton's law of universal gravitation and use it, and describe Kepler's laws.

sections.title: Introduction to Uniform Circular Motion and Gravitation
objectives: Describe what makes circular motion different from motion in a straight line.

misconceptions.claim: In circular motion the object is accelerating because it is going round a corner.
misconceptions.correction: That is right. Its direction keeps changing, and a change of direction is a change of velocity, which is an acceleration.

summary: Circular motion is accelerated motion, because the direction of the velocity keeps changing.
Uniform circular motion has a constant speed and a constant centripetal acceleration.
The force that does it always points to the centre.
sections.no_worked_example_reason: The source carries no worked example for this section and no solved exercise to promote, so the practice is left to the exercises themselves.

sections.title: Rotation Angle and Angular Velocity
objectives: Define the rotation angle, the angular velocity and the angular acceleration.
Convert between angular and linear quantities at a radius.

misconceptions.claim: The angular velocity of a wheel is the same everywhere on the wheel.
misconceptions.correction: The linear speed is larger the further out you are, but the angle turned per second is the same for every point on the wheel.

summary: The rotation angle is measured in radians.
Angular velocity is the rate at which the angle changes.
The linear speed at a radius is the angular speed times the radius.

sections.title: Centripetal Acceleration
objectives: Define centripetal acceleration and give its size and its direction.
Derive the centripetal acceleration from the components of the acceleration.

misconceptions.claim: Centripetal acceleration pushes the object outward, away from the centre.
misconceptions.correction: It points inward. The inward acceleration is exactly what is needed to keep the object on the circle.

summary: Centripetal acceleration always points to the centre of the circle.
Its size is the square of the speed over the radius.
It exists only while the object is turning.

sections.title: Centripetal Force
objectives: Compute the centripetal force and give its direction.
Explain which forces combine to make it.

misconceptions.claim: Centripetal force is a new kind of force that pulls objects to the centre.
misconceptions.correction: It is not a new force at all. It is the name for the net inward force that an existing force, such as tension or friction, provides.

summary: The centripetal force is the net force pointing to the centre.
Its size is mass times the centripetal acceleration.
Whatever force supplies it, gravity, tension or friction, the object stays on the circle.

sections.title: Fictitious Forces and Non-inertial Frames: The Coriolis Force
objectives: Describe what changes for an observer in an accelerating frame.
Explain the Coriolis force that a rotating observer feels.

misconceptions.claim: If you feel a force, then there is a real force acting on you.
misconceptions.correction: In an accelerating or rotating frame the observer feels a force that the observer's own frame has invented. That is why a turn feels like a push.

summary: An accelerating frame has its own fictitious forces.
A rotating frame adds the Coriolis force, which depends on the direction of the motion.
The laws of physics are simplest in an inertial frame.
sections.no_worked_example_reason: The source carries no worked example for this section and no solved exercise to promote, so the practice is left to the exercises themselves.

sections.title: Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation
objectives: State Newton's law of universal gravitation and use it.
Find the acceleration due to gravity at the surface of a body.

misconceptions.claim: Gravity pulls harder on a heavy object than on a light one.
misconceptions.correction: The force is larger, but so is the mass that has to be accelerated. The acceleration due to gravity at the surface is the same for every object, whatever its mass.

summary: The gravitational force falls off with the square of the distance.
The force on a small mass near a large one is small, but the acceleration is large.
g at the surface of the Earth is about 9.8 m/s², and it is the same for every falling object.

sections.title: Satellites and Kepler's Laws: An Argument for Simplicity
objectives: State Kepler's three laws of planetary motion.
Explain why a satellite stays in orbit.

misconceptions.claim: A satellite is held up by the engine that keeps it flying.
misconceptions.correction: Most of them coast. They fall towards the Earth while moving sideways fast enough to keep missing it, and that falling is the orbit.

summary: An orbit is a fall that keeps missing the ground.
Kepler's first law says planets travel in ellipses with the Sun at one focus.
The third law ties the period of an orbit to the size of the orbit.

exam_traps.subject: physics
exam_traps.misconception: When the distance between two bodies doubles, the gravitational pull halves.
exam_traps.correction: The force varies with the inverse square of the distance, so doubling the distance leaves a quarter of the force.
exam_traps.signal: The paper offers the halved force as an option, and the answer is the quarter.

exam_traps.subject: physics
exam_traps.misconception: Doubling both masses leaves the gravitational force between them unchanged.
exam_traps.correction: The force is proportional to the product of the masses, so doubling both of them multiplies the force by four.
exam_traps.signal: The paper offers the unchanged force as an option, and the answer is four times as large.

exam_traps.subject: physics
exam_traps.misconception: The angular speed of an object moving in a circle is the linear speed times the radius.
exam_traps.correction: The angular speed is the linear speed divided by the radius, so it is the same for every point on the rim.
exam_traps.signal: The paper offers the product of the linear speed and the radius as an option.

exam_traps.subject: physics
exam_traps.misconception: Centripetal acceleration pushes the object outward, away from the centre.
exam_traps.correction: It points inward. The inward acceleration is what keeps the object on the circle.
exam_traps.signal: Our own question offers the outward direction as an option.

exam_traps.subject: physics
exam_traps.misconception: Centripetal force is a new kind of force that pulls objects to the centre.
exam_traps.correction: It is the name for the net inward force, whatever provides it: gravity, tension or friction.
exam_traps.signal: Our own question offers the new force as an option.

exam_traps.subject: physics
exam_traps.misconception: A satellite is held up by the engine that keeps it flying.
exam_traps.correction: Most of them coast. A satellite falls towards the Earth while moving sideways fast enough to keep missing it.
exam_traps.signal: Our own question offers the engine as the answer.

exam_traps.subject: physics
exam_traps.misconception: A heavier body feels a greater pull from the Earth.
exam_traps.correction: Every body on the Earth feels the same pull per unit mass. The weight of a body on the Moon is one sixth of its weight on the Earth, whatever its mass.
exam_traps.signal: Our own question offers the same weight as an option.

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: A wheel of radius 0.5 m turns at 4 rad/s. What is the linear speed of a point on the rim?
exam_recall_checks.explanation: The linear speed is v = ωr = 4 × 0.5 = 2 m/s.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the WAEC physics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: The gravitational force between two bodies is 5 N. What is the force when the distance between them is halved?
exam_recall_checks.explanation: The force varies with the inverse square of the distance, so halving the distance multiplies the force by four, giving 20 N.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the JAMB physics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: A wheel of radius 1 m turns at 2 rad/s. What is the linear speed at the rim?
exam_recall_checks.explanation: The linear speed is $v = \omega r = 2 \times 1 = 2$ m/s.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the JAMB physics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: A car travels at 20 m/s round a circle of radius 50 m. What is its centripetal acceleration?
exam_recall_checks.explanation: The centripetal acceleration is $a = v^2/r = 400/50 = 8$ m/s².
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the WAEC physics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: A 1000 kg car goes round a bend of radius 100 m at 20 m/s. What centripetal force is needed?
exam_recall_checks.explanation: The centripetal force is $F = mv^2/r = 1000 \times 400/100 = 4000$ N.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the WAEC physics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: The gravitational force between two bodies is 9 N. If one of the masses is doubled, the force becomes
exam_recall_checks.explanation: The force is proportional to the product of the masses, so doubling one mass doubles the force.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the WAEC physics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: A satellite in a lower orbit moves faster than one in a higher orbit because

options.text: the gravitational field is stronger there
the satellite has a greater mass

exam_recall_checks.explanation: The orbital speed grows as the radius shrinks, so a lower orbit is a faster one.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the WAEC physics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: A car travels at 20 m/s round a circle of radius 50 m. What is the centripetal acceleration?
exam_recall_checks.explanation: The centripetal acceleration is $v^2/r = 400/50 = 8$ m/s², directed to the centre.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the WAEC physics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: A 1000 kg car goes round a bend of radius 100 m at 20 m/s. What centripetal force is needed?
exam_recall_checks.explanation: The centripetal force is $F = mv^2/r = 1000 \times 400/100 = 4000$ N, supplied by the friction between the tyres and the road.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the WAEC physics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: A satellite moves in a circular orbit. What holds it in that orbit?

options.text: Its forward motion, which makes it keep falling past the Earth
The pull of the Earth alone, with no motion
The air high above the atmosphere

exam_recall_checks.explanation: An orbit is a fall that keeps missing the ground. The forward motion carries the satellite sideways while gravity pulls it inward.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the WAEC physics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: A body has a weight of 60 N on the Earth. What is its weight on the Moon?
exam_recall_checks.explanation: The Moon's pull is one sixth of the Earth's, so the weight is 60/6 = 10 N. The mass has not changed.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the WAEC physics syllabus
